eligibility.evidence: Open-source LLMs given the prisoner's dilemma with stake size and the traveler's dilemma with penalty size; human findings cited (Yamagishi et al. 2016; Basu 1994; Morone et al. 2014). Preference probabilities are new behaviour (Results, pp. 3-5).

A.title: Do Large Language Models Learn Human-Like Strategic Preferences?
A.venue: REALM 2025 workshop (ACL Anthology DOI); text read is the arXiv v2 copy

paradigms.name: Prisoner's dilemma with stake size (shared air conditioner vs life support scenarios)
paradigms.source_paper: Yamagishi et al. 2016 (stake-size effect in humans)
paradigms.location: Section 'Do LLMs Have Human-Like Preference in the Prisoner's Dilemma?', Table 2, Fig. 3

paradigms.name: Traveler's dilemma with penalty size (2 vs 20; quoting 99 vs 100)
paradigms.source_paper: Basu 1994; Morone et al. 2014; Becker et al. 2004
paradigms.location: Section 'Do LLMs Have Human-Like Preference in the Traveler's Dilemma?', Fig. 4

D.metric: qualitative direction of cooperation vs betrayal (PD) and indifference vs preference for 99 (TD) against cited human findings

effects.label: SAME-DIRECTION-UNQUANTIFIED
effects.location: Results PD, Fig. 3; Wilcoxon preference relation, Table 3

effects.label: SAME-DIRECTION-UNQUANTIFIED
effects.location: Results PD, Fig. 3 (strong cooperation at low stakes, partial self-interest at high stakes; authors call the model brittle)

effects.label: INSUFFICIENT
effects.location: Results PD, Fig. 3 (uncertain preference at low stakes, partial self-interest at high stakes; no stake-effect verdict)

effects.label: SAME-DIRECTION-UNQUANTIFIED

E.headline: Solar and Mistral show human-like cooperation in the PD (with stake size) and TD (with penalty size); larger models have value-based preferences; most large models are brittle.

G.notes: 19 model species were screened but only 5 are named in the text; the appendix with all prompts is cited but is absent from the markdown (f4 coded from the paper's statement). Responses are word probabilities, not sampled text. Human data are cited findings only; no human sample size or effect size.
